directAnswer: Pope Martin IV was Simon de Brion, a French cardinal and former chancellor of King Louis IX, who reigned from 22 February 1281 to 28 March 1285. Closely allied with Charles of Anjou, he broke with the Byzantine emperor, and after the Sicilian Vespers revolt of 1282 he excommunicated Peter III of Aragon and proclaimed the Aragonese Crusade.

sections.h2: Simon de Brion, Royal Chancellor and Legate
paras: Simon was born in the region of Brie in France and served King Louis IX as keeper of the seals, or chancellor. Urban IV created him a cardinal in 1261. As papal legate in France he handled the negotiations that brought Charles of Anjou to accept the crown of Sicily, and he later helped prepare the process for the canonization of Louis IX.

His election at Viterbo in February 1281 came after a six-month vacancy and under strong pressure from Charles of Anjou, whose supporters had disrupted the conclave. The people of Rome nonetheless named him senator of the city, an office he delegated to Charles.

sections.h2: Why He Was Called Martin the Fourth
paras: Only one earlier pope, St. Martin I, had actually borne the name Martin. However, medieval scribes had confused the name of the popes Marinus I and Marinus II with Martin, and so Simon took the number four. The official numbering has kept that count ever since.

sections.h2: The Sicilian Vespers and the Aragonese Crusade
paras: Martin's policy followed Charles of Anjou's interests closely. In 1281 he excommunicated the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII, whom Charles intended to attack, effectively ending the reunion proclaimed at the Second Council of Lyon. Charles's eastern plans collapsed, however, when Sicily rose against Angevin rule in the revolt known as the Sicilian Vespers, which began at Palermo on Easter Monday, 30 March 1282.

The Sicilians offered the crown to Peter III of Aragon, whose wife was Manfred's daughter. Martin excommunicated Peter, declared his kingdom forfeit, and offered Aragon to Charles of Valois, a son of King Philip III of France. He granted crusade status to the war that followed. The French invasion of Aragon in 1285 ended in failure, and Sicily remained under Aragonese rule.

Unrest in Rome kept Martin in Orvieto and Perugia, where he was crowned and where he spent his reign. He granted the mendicant friars broad rights to preach and hear confessions with the bull Ad fructus uberes in 1281, which caused friction with diocesan clergy.

He died at Perugia on 28 March 1285 and was buried in its cathedral. Dante placed him in Purgatory among the gluttons, mentioning his fondness for eels from Lake Bolsena, a poetic detail rather than a documented record.

keyFacts: Born Simon de Brion in Brie, France; chancellor to King Louis IX
Elected at Viterbo in 1281 with the backing of Charles of Anjou
Excommunicated Michael VIII, ending the union of Lyon
Reigned during the Sicilian Vespers (1282) and declared the Aragonese Crusade
Numbered IV because the two popes Marinus were miscounted as Martin

faqs.question: What were the Sicilian Vespers?
faqs.answer: A revolt against Angevin French rule that began in Palermo on 30 March 1282. The Sicilians turned to Peter III of Aragon, and Martin IV responded by excommunicating Peter and supporting a French war against Aragon.

faqs.question: Why is he Martin IV if there were only two earlier Martins?
faqs.answer: Medieval lists confused the popes Marinus I and Marinus II with Martin, so Simon de Brion counted himself the fourth Martin. The numbering was kept.

faqs.question: Did Martin IV ever live in Rome?
faqs.answer: No. Because of unrest in the city, he resided at Orvieto and Perugia throughout his pontificate.
